channel.description: Recent content in Publishing on Pandaqi Tutorials

item.title: Introduction
item.description: Welcome to this course on publishing. It assumes you have some (written) work that you would like to publish. Before we start, I must admit that (at the time of writing) I am mostly self-published. I usually do all the steps in the process of publishing a finished book and know all the ins and outs of self publishing.

item.title: The Two Hats
item.description: A writer who wishes to have a long, sustainable career has to wear two different hats. The first hat is obviously the writer’s hat. You put it on for weeks or months to get that story out and finish the book. The second hat is the business hat. That’s the one necessary when trying to get your work published and making an income from it.

item.title: How to Sell your Work I
item.description: In the previous chapter, I told you to put on the Business Hat (and take off the Writer’s Hat). In doing so, you need to turn your carefully written book into something fit for marketing or selling.

item.title: How to Sell your Work II
item.description: Previous chapter asked you to pin down your target audience and your unique selling point. This chapter is more about the specific content of your book and the marketing text you’ll add.

item.title: Traditional Publishing
item.description: This article talks about the pros and cons of traditional publishing, how the process works (in general, specific chapters come later), and the role literary agents play in there.

item.title: Query Letters
item.description: Query letters follow a relatively strict format. It’s not that you’re required to follow it, or that it’s some unwritten rule. It’s simply the easiest and fastest way to get your point across, and agents like to see it that way. If you receive 10 unsolicited manuscripts every day, you want their query letter to follow the same structure, because it makes your job a thousand times easier.

item.title: Synopsis
item.description: The synopsis has always been my biggest struggle. The first drafts of my stories tend to become overly complicated, with too many story threads, which makes it impossible to summarize it all in a single page.

item.title: Self-Publishing I
item.description: Earlier in the course, I discussed how traditional publishing works, plus its advantages or disadvantages. I also confessed I don’t have much experience with that. (Lots of experience submitting and being rejected—also for writing contests—but not actually getting accepted.)

item.title: Self-Publishing II
item.description: As promised, in this article I’ll give my reviews of the most popular self-publishing services. Where possible, I’ll include practical tips on how to use them, plus my personal statistics/data from using them.

item.title: Cover Design
item.description: Obviously, this course is not about graphic design or illustration. This chapter merely gives some basic advice on how to approach creating the right cover, using tips that anyone can execute (regardless of skill or expertise).

item.title: File Formats
item.description:
When it comes to publishing, services generally accept or output 4 formats.

  • Word documents (.doc or .docx)
  • PDF documents (.pdf)
  • EPUB documents (.epub, maybe .mobi)

Microsoft Word

Many writers, especially those that just start out, simply create their novels in Word. This is fine. Unless you have special requirements, this is all you need.

item.title: Conclusion
item.description:
Congratulations on finishing the course about publishing!

Hopefully it gave useful advice about how to sell and market a book, whether it’s to a literary agent (to get published traditionally) or to your audience (when self-publishing). It’s all about removing the Writer’s Hat and putting on the Business Hat. To see your book as a product that needs to be marketed, and to make the (sometimes harsh) decisions necessary to accomplish that.
